statements.text: Exploring the expressive arts is essential to developing artistic skills and knowledge and it enables learners to become curious and creative individuals.
Responding and reflecting, both as artist and audience, is a fundamental part of learning in the expressive arts.
Creating combines skills and knowledge, drawing on the senses, inspiration and imagination.
Developing physical health and well-being has lifelong benefits.
How we process and respond to our experiences affects our mental health and emotional well-being.
Our decision-making impacts on the quality of our lives and the lives of others.
How we engage with social influences shapes who we are and affects our health and well-being.
Healthy relationships are fundamental to our well-being.
Enquiry, exploration and investigation inspire curiosity about the world, its past, present and future.
Events and human experiences are complex, and are perceived, interpreted and represented in different ways.
Our natural world is diverse and dynamic, influenced by processes and human actions.
Human societies are complex and diverse, and shaped by human actions and beliefs.
Informed, self-aware citizens engage with the challenges and opportunities that face humanity, and are able to take considered and ethical action.
Languages connect us.
Understanding languages is key to understanding the world around us.
Expressing ourselves through languages is key to communication.
Literature fires imagination and inspires creativity.
The number system is used to represent and compare relationships between numbers and quantities.
Algebra uses symbol systems to express the structure of mathematical relationships.
Geometry focuses on relationships involving shape, space and position, and measurement focuses on quantifying phenomena in the physical world.
Statistics represent data, probability models chance, and both support informed inferences and decisions.
Being curious and searching for answers is essential to understanding and predicting phenomena.
Design thinking and engineering offer technical and creative ways to meet society’s needs and wants.
The world around us is full of living things which depend on each other for survival.
Matter and the way it behaves defines our universe and shapes our lives.
Forces and energy provide a foundation for understanding our universe.
Computation is the foundation for our digital world.

records.statement: Exploring the expressive arts is essential to developing artistic skills and knowledge and it enables learners to become curious and creative individuals.
records.descriptor: I can explore and experiment with and then select appropriate creative techniques, practices, materials, processes, resources, tools and technologies.

ideas.resources: Chromebook or iPad with Scratch
ideas.title: Interactive Model - selecting and controlling creative techniques and materials
ideas.description: Pupils test different techniques and record the effect each produces. They turn it into a simple interactive model or quiz. They test it with a partner, find one mistake or unclear part and improve it. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to test different techniques and record the effect each produces.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how combining two techniques changes the effect of a creative piece. Pupils build a simple clickable model or quiz, ask a partner to test it and fix one part that is confusing or incorrect.

ideas.resources: A3 paper, pens, sticky notes and success criteria. Include safe creative materials suited to the chosen discipline.
ideas.title: Gallery Walk and Improve - selecting and controlling creative techniques and materials
ideas.description: Pupils compare traditional and digital processes for the same creative purpose. They display a first version of their work. Other pupils share one thing that works well and ask one helpful question. Pupils then improve one part and explain their change. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to compare traditional and digital processes for the same creative purpose.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how combining two techniques changes the effect of a creative piece. Pupils display their first attempt around the room. Classmates leave one helpful comment, then everyone chooses one change to make.

records.statement: Exploring the expressive arts is essential to developing artistic skills and knowledge and it enables learners to become curious and creative individuals.
records.descriptor: I can explore how and why creative work is made by asking questions and developing my own answers.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Slides or PowerPoint Online
ideas.title: Collaborative Source Board - developing and refining a creative design
ideas.description: Groups produce two possible designs and combine their strongest features. They use a small set of sources chosen by the teacher. Each pupil adds one evidence card. The group sorts the cards and agrees on a conclusion based on what they found. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to produce two possible designs and combine their strongest features.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how feedback could improve a planned character, product or performance. Each pupil adds one useful fact or example to a shared board. The group sorts the evidence and agrees on a conclusion based on what they found.

ideas.resources: A3 paper, pens, sticky notes and success criteria. Include safe creative materials suited to the chosen discipline.
ideas.title: Gallery Walk and Improve - developing and refining a creative design
ideas.description: Pupils document how an idea changes from first sketch to final outcome. They display a first version of their work. Other pupils share one thing that works well and ask one helpful question. Pupils then improve one part and explain their change. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to document how an idea changes from first sketch to final outcome.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how feedback could improve a planned character, product or performance. Pupils display their first attempt around the room. Classmates leave one helpful comment, then everyone chooses one change to make.

records.statement: Exploring the expressive arts is essential to developing artistic skills and knowledge and it enables learners to become curious and creative individuals.
records.descriptor: I can explore and describe how artists and creative work communicate mood, feelings and ideas.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Slides or PowerPoint Online
ideas.title: Collaborative Source Board - how creative choices communicate mood and feeling
ideas.description: Groups transform the same idea to communicate two different moods. They use a small set of sources chosen by the teacher. Each pupil adds one evidence card. The group sorts the cards and agrees on a conclusion based on what they found. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to transform the same idea to communicate two different moods.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how music, movement or camera angle can change the mood of a short scene. Each pupil adds one useful fact or example to a shared board. The group sorts the evidence and agrees on a conclusion based on what they found.

ideas.resources: challenge cards, cones or table markers and feedback slips. Include safe creative materials suited to the chosen discipline.
ideas.title: Paired Coaching Circuit - how creative choices communicate mood and feeling
ideas.description: Pairs match different creative choices to feelings and explain the matches. They work through a few short challenges. One pupil completes or explains the task while the other checks one success point. They then swap roles and improve. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to match different creative choices to feelings and explain the matches.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how music, movement or camera angle can change the mood of a short scene. At each short station, one pupil completes or explains the task while their partner checks one success point. They swap roles and try to improve.

records.statement: Exploring the expressive arts is essential to developing artistic skills and knowledge and it enables learners to become curious and creative individuals.
records.descriptor: I can explore and experiment independently and demonstrate technical control with a range of creative materials, processes, resources, tools and technologies showing innovation and resilience.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Docs or Google Slides
ideas.title: Digital Peer Review - creative problem-solving and resilience
ideas.description: Pupils choose a strategy for staying flexible when a creative plan does not work. They share a draft with a partner, who points out one strength and one useful improvement. They decide which feedback to use and briefly explain why. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to choose a strategy for staying flexible when a creative plan does not work.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how an artist or designer can respond when materials, time or technology create a problem. Partners share a first draft online and add one positive comment and one suggestion. Each pupil uses the most helpful feedback and briefly explains the change.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Slides or PowerPoint Online
ideas.title: Explainer Presentation - creative problem-solving and resilience
ideas.description: Teams choose a strategy for staying flexible when a creative plan does not work. They create four simple slides showing the question, evidence, explanation and conclusion. Another pair suggests one improvement, which they use to make their work clearer. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to choose a strategy for staying flexible when a creative plan does not work.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how an artist or designer can respond when materials, time or technology create a problem. Groups use four slides: the question, an example, their explanation and a conclusion. Another group checks whether the message is easy to follow.

records.statement: Exploring the expressive arts is essential to developing artistic skills and knowledge and it enables learners to become curious and creative individuals.
records.descriptor: I can explore the effects that a range of creative techniques, materials, processes, resources, tools and technologies have on my own and others’ creative work.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Scratch
ideas.title: Scratch Simulation - selecting and controlling creative techniques and materials
ideas.description: Pupils compare traditional and digital processes for the same creative purpose. They make a simple model that lets people try different choices. They explain what they have assumed, try different choices and discuss how the model is different from real life. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to compare traditional and digital processes for the same creative purpose.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how deliberate control of techniques and materials can achieve a chosen outcome. Pupils build a simple Scratch model with choices or changing values. They try different inputs and discuss how the model is similar to and different from real life.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with a browser-based recorder or Voice Recorder
ideas.title: Podcast Panel - selecting and controlling creative techniques and materials
ideas.description: Groups compare traditional and digital processes for the same creative purpose. Give each pupil a different opinion to share, then record a two-minute discussion. They end by agreeing on what worked, what could improve and one question they still have. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to compare traditional and digital processes for the same creative purpose.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how deliberate control of techniques and materials can achieve a chosen outcome. Give each group member a different opinion to explore and record a two-minute discussion. The group finishes by agreeing on what the evidence shows and one question they still have.

records.statement: Exploring the expressive arts is essential to developing artistic skills and knowledge and it enables learners to become curious and creative individuals.
records.descriptor: I can explore how creative work can represent, document, share and celebrate personal, social and cultural identities.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Slides or Scratch
ideas.title: Branching Decision Model - presenting creative work for an audience
ideas.description: Pupils rehearse, present and review how an audience responds. They make a choose-your-own-path diagram. For each choice, they show what might happen, the evidence behind it and how the decision could be changed. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to rehearse, present and review how an audience responds.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how a venue, platform and audience could shape the presentation of creative work. Pupils begin with one situation and add at least three possible choices. Each branch shows what might happen next and the reason behind it.

ideas.resources: task cards, practical materials suited to the topic and mini whiteboards. Include safe creative materials suited to the chosen discipline.
ideas.title: Expert Stations - presenting creative work for an audience
ideas.description: Groups adapt one creative decision to make the intended message clearer. They work through a few short activity stations. At the end, each group teaches one example to the class and asks a quick checking question. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to adapt one creative decision to make the intended message clearer.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how a venue, platform and audience could shape the presentation of creative work. Groups complete different short stations and become the class expert on one example. They then teach it to others and ask one quick checking question.

ideas.description: Pupils compare how thoughts, feelings and actions can influence one another. They create a short digital field-guide entry. They combine a labelled picture, short text and an optional voice recording. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to compare how thoughts, feelings and actions can influence one another.
ideas.example: For example, pupils could explore which strategies could help someone manage anger or disappointment. Pupils create one field-guide page using a labelled image, a short explanation and an optional voice recording. A partner checks it for clarity.

ideas.resources: A3 paper, pens, sticky notes and success criteria. Use fictional scenarios; no personal disclosure is required.
ideas.title: Gallery Walk and Improve - recognising and managing feelings
ideas.description: Pupils compare how thoughts, feelings and actions can influence one another. They display a first version of their work. Other pupils share one thing that works well and ask one helpful question. Pupils then improve one part and explain their change. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to compare how thoughts, feelings and actions can influence one another.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore which strategies could help someone manage anger or disappointment. Pupils display their first attempt around the room. Classmates leave one helpful comment, then everyone chooses one change to make.

ideas.resources: iPad or Chromebook with a voice recorder
ideas.title: Audio Field Report - recognising and managing feelings
ideas.description: Small groups build a bank of strategies for different levels of emotion, plan a one-minute audio report and include an observation, an explanation and a conclusion. A partner checks that the examples support the main message. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to build a bank of strategies for different levels of emotion.
ideas.example: For example, pupils could explore which strategies could help someone manage anger or disappointment. Pairs record a one-minute report with an introduction, two useful pieces of evidence and a conclusion. They listen back and improve the least clear part.

ideas.resources: fictional scenario cards, role badges and consequence cards. Use fictional scenarios; no personal disclosure is required.
ideas.title: Role-Play Decisions - recognising and managing feelings
ideas.description: Groups build a bank of strategies for different levels of emotion. They act out a simple made-up situation. They pause at each choice, discuss what might happen and replay the scene using a better choice. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to build a bank of strategies for different levels of emotion.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore which strategies could help someone manage anger or disappointment. Groups act out a short made-up situation and pause whenever a choice is needed. They discuss what may happen, replay the scene with a different choice and compare the results.

ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how a class-library system could sort, store and find books. Pupils build a simple clickable model or quiz, ask a partner to test it and fix one part that is confusing or incorrect.

records.statement: Computation is the foundation for our digital world.
records.descriptor: I can follow instructions to build and control a physical device.

ideas.resources: iPad or Chromebook with Google Slides or PowerPoint Online
ideas.title: Evidence Slide Deck - computational thinking, data and connected systems
ideas.description: Pairs create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome. They make three slides showing their evidence, explanation and conclusion. They add captions and arrows, then swap with another pair and suggest one improvement. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how a class-library system could sort, store and find books. Pairs make three slides showing their evidence, what it means and their conclusion. They swap with another pair and use one suggestion to improve it.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Slides or PowerPoint Online
ideas.title: Collaborative Source Board - computational thinking, data and connected systems
ideas.description: Groups create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome. They use a small set of sources chosen by the teacher. Each pupil adds one evidence card. The group sorts the cards and agrees on a conclusion based on what they found. Pairs compare their work and explain how it meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how a class-library system could sort, store and find books. Each pupil adds one useful fact or example to a shared board. The group sorts the evidence and agrees on a conclusion based on what they found.

records.statement: Computation is the foundation for our digital world.
records.descriptor: I can use conditional statements to add control and decision-making to algorithms.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Docs or Google Slides
ideas.title: Digital Peer Review - computational thinking, data and connected systems
ideas.description: Pupils create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome. They share a draft with a partner, who points out one strength and one useful improvement. They decide which feedback to use and briefly explain why. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how an app could collect useful data while protecting the user's privacy. Partners share a first draft online and add one positive comment and one suggestion. Each pupil uses the most helpful feedback and briefly explains the change.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Scratch
ideas.title: Scratch Simulation - computational thinking, data and connected systems
ideas.description: Pupils create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome. They make a simple model that lets people try different choices. They explain what they have assumed, try different choices and discuss how the model is different from real life. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to create, run and debug an algorithm for a clear outcome.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how an app could collect useful data while protecting the user's privacy. Pupils build a simple Scratch model with choices or changing values. They try different inputs and discuss how the model is similar to and different from real life.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Docs or Microsoft Word Online
ideas.title: Source Audit - computational thinking, data and connected systems
ideas.description: Pupils look at an app screen or set of data and make it clearer or more accurate. They use two sources chosen by the teacher. They label the main points and supporting evidence, noting anything they are unsure about. They then write a short conclusion and mention one limitation. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to look at an app screen or set of data and make it clearer or more accurate.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how an app could collect useful data while protecting the user's privacy. Pupils highlight the main claim and the evidence that supports it in two short sources. They note anything uncertain before writing a balanced conclusion.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Sheets or Excel Online
ideas.title: Data Story - computational thinking, data and connected systems
ideas.description: Pupils look at an app screen or set of data and make it clearer or more accurate. They use a small set of relevant data. They choose a suitable calculation or chart, explain the pattern and check whether the visual might give the wrong impression. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to look at an app screen or set of data and make it clearer or more accurate.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how an app could collect useful data while protecting the user's privacy. Pupils choose a suitable calculation, table or chart and add a short explanation of the pattern. They also check whether the visual could give the wrong impression.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Slides or Scratch
ideas.title: Branching Decision Model - computational thinking, data and connected systems
ideas.description: Pupils replace repeated instructions with a loop or conditional decision. They make a choose-your-own-path diagram. For each choice, they show what might happen, the evidence behind it and how the decision could be changed. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to replace repeated instructions with a loop or conditional decision.
ideas.example: One classroom example is to explore how an app could collect useful data while protecting the user's privacy. Pupils begin with one situation and add at least three possible choices. Each branch shows what might happen next and the reason behind it.

ideas.resources: Chromebook with Google Slides or PowerPoint Online
ideas.title: Explainer Presentation - computational thinking, data and connected systems
ideas.description: Teams replace repeated instructions with a loop or conditional decision. They create four simple slides showing the question, evidence, explanation and conclusion. Another pair suggests one improvement, which they use to make their work clearer. Pupils then explain the choices they made and how well their final work meets the learning goal.
ideas.learningGoal: Pupils will learn to replace repeated instructions with a loop or conditional decision.
ideas.example: This activity could focus on how an app could collect useful data while protecting the user's privacy. Groups use four slides: the question, an example, their explanation and a conclusion. Another group checks whether the message is easy to follow.
